assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform in which a single tuning parameter, the twist angle, produces flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a clean two-dimensional material. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted the flat-band angle from electronic-structure reasoning, and the 2018 experiments confirmed it. This unusually clean theory-to-experiment chain, and the field it opened in moire quantum matter, is very attractive from a theoretical materials perspective.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical prediction is credited to Bistritzer and MacDonald and the decisive experimental demonstration to Jarillo-Herrero (with his group). That is a natural three-person configuration. Other contributors to early moire band theory (for example Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) and to the experimental programme are not in the credited list, so credit around the theory is not fully settled.
assessment.maturity: Several independent groups reproduced correlated states and superconductivity within a few years, and the continuum-model picture is widely adopted. The origin of superconductivity and the detailed role of interactions remain debated, so the interpretation is not fully settled. Timing is reasonable but the field is still young.
uncertainties: Microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still contested.
Earlier moire band-structure work by others may complicate the theory attribution.
Sample-to-sample variation and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect introduced a new classification of band insulators by topological invariants, with protected edge or surface states. The Kane-Mele proposal, followed by the HgTe quantum-well realisation, changed how band structure is understood across materials physics. Importance, originality and lasting impact are very high and the concept is clean.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the decisive Z2 theory of the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene; Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental observation in HgTe wells following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. The credited trio supports a fair configuration, though the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (Zhang is deceased) and of the three-dimensional topological insulator contributors leaves some allocation question.
assessment.maturity: The effect has been confirmed independently in many materials and angle-resolved and transport signatures are well understood. Recognition is mature and arguably overdue, though it comes with a crowded and overlapping credit landscape.
uncertainties: Allocation between the two-dimensional and three-dimensional topological insulator contributions is unresolved.
Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction is not among the credited names.
Graphene itself has too small a spin-orbit gap to realise the original proposal.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the central modern framework for strongly correlated electrons, solving the Mott transition and, in combination with density functional theory, enabling realistic treatment of correlated materials. It is a controlled limit (infinite dimensions) that became a practical computational tool with broad use in transition-metal oxides, f-electron systems and spectroscopy. I regard its methodological impact on materials theory as substantial and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimensional limit, Georges and Kotliar mapped it onto a self-consistent impurity problem, and Muller-Hartmann also contributed (deceased). Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt is a plausible three-person set, but Metzner's role and the earlier impurity-solver lineage make the attribution contestable.
assessment.maturity: The method is mature and validated in many comparisons with experiments, though quantitative accuracy for real materials depends on the impurity solver, double-counting corrections and choice of correlated subspace. Recognition is timely, but the Prize emphasis on discoveries over methods is a consideration.
uncertainties: Whether a theoretical method fits the physics prize as a discovery or invention.
Metzner's and Muller-Hartmann's credit.
Quantitative predictive reliability for real materials varies.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetic skyrmions are topologically protected spin textures that link magnetism, topology and spintronics. Observation of the skyrmion lattice in MnSi and real-space imaging, then room-temperature and single-skyrmion control, established a rich field. This is squarely in my area of magnetism and spin dynamics, and the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya-driven stabilisation is well understood in atomistic and continuum theory.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer (with Muhlbauer, Boni and co-workers) found the lattice in MnSi, Tokura's group provided real-space imaging in insulating and metallic systems, and Wiesendanger's group demonstrated individual atomic-scale skyrmions. The theoretical foundation by Bogdanov and Rossler is not in the credited names, which leaves the credit allocation open.
assessment.maturity: The phenomenon is confirmed by many independent groups, but application impact (racetrack memory, neuromorphic devices) has not matured. Fundamental discovery is strong; the interpretation of device-relevant dynamics is still evolving.
uncertainties: Theoretical originators (Bogdanov, Rossler) are absent from the credited names.
Technological promise is unproven.
Priority split between bulk lattice and interfacial skyrmions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Giant tunnel magnetoresistance in MgO-based magnetic tunnel junctions delivered large room-temperature signals, driven by coherent spin-dependent tunnelling through symmetry-filtered Bloch states. It combined first-principles prediction with experiment and underpins hard-drive read heads and MRAM, extending the 2007 recognition of giant magnetoresistance. From my perspective the first-principles prediction is an especially clean example of electronic-structure theory guiding discovery.
assessment.attribution: Butler and Mathon predicted the coherent tunnelling effect; Parkin and Yuasa independently demonstrated large effects in MgO junctions in 2004. Miyazaki (and Moodera for earlier room-temperature TMR) is credited elsewhere, so I picked the theory-plus-two-experiments configuration; the alternative of including Miyazaki and Moodera leaves a genuine credit dispute.
assessment.maturity: The effect is thoroughly confirmed and commercially deployed. Recognition is mature, although some may see it as a continuation of the GMR prize.
uncertainties: Priority among Miyazaki, Moodera, Parkin and Yuasa.
Overlap with the 2007 GMR prize.
Mathon is not among the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC confirmed the last missing Standard Model particle and the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking, a landmark in physics. The 2013 prize recognised theory only, so the experimental side remains unrecognised.
assessment.attribution: The discovery was a collaborative effort of thousands of people; the credited spokespersons and project leaders (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) represent leadership of ATLAS and CMS, but whether they fit the 'decisive contributions' standard is a recognised difficulty. Fabiola Gianotti and Joe Incandela as announcing spokespersons also feature in the debate.
assessment.maturity: The result is extensively confirmed and its properties are measured in increasing detail. Timeliness is fine. The principal obstacle is attribution rather than maturity.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration credit is difficult to assign to three people.
Whether leadership roles equal decisive scientific contribution.
Prior prize in 2013 already recognised the mechanism.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model in a controlled setting, with the Mott insulator transition and later quantum gas microscopy, giving access to correlated many-body physics and quantum simulation. This is of direct interest to me because it tests the model Hamiltonians that condensed-matter theory relies on, with tunable parameters.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller proposed the Hubbard realisation, Greiner (with Bloch and Hansch) observed the Mott transition, and Bloch and Greiner developed quantum gas microscopy. The configuration of Zoller, Bloch and Greiner is reasonable though Cirac, Jaksch and Hansch's roles are debatable; the list includes four credited names.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely replicated, although its largest impact on solving open materials problems is still in the future. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Boundary with the recognised 2001 BEC and 2012 prizes.
Credit among Zoller, Jaksch, Cirac, Bloch and Greiner.
Practical advantage over classical simulation remains to be shown.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: ARPES on cuprates mapped the Fermi surface, d-wave gap, pseudogap and nodal quasiparticle dispersions of high-temperature superconductors, directly connecting measured spectra to many-body theory. As someone who stresses understanding why spectra look the way they do, I value this, though the discovery is a technique-driven body of measurement rather than one decisive finding.
assessment.attribution: Campuzano, Shen and Takahashi are leading experimental contributors; credit is spread across many groups and instrument developers (including photoemission pioneers), so a compact three-person allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Results are confirmed by many groups, but the central problem of the pairing mechanism remains unresolved, and the Prize may be viewed as premature or incomplete with respect to a conclusive physical result.
uncertainties: The mechanism of cuprate superconductivity is still open.
Credit distribution among many ARPES groups.
Whether this is a discovery or a technique.
